title: Judaism: study is holy
hook: learning is itself worship, and argument is honored (Pirkei Avot 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: brit, covenant, a people bound to God by a promise. Your line was a promise kept. Which small promise did you keep? Day two hundred forty-eight.

Picture a room full of long tables. Two people sit across from each other with one big book open between them, and they are arguing. Not whispering. Arguing, out loud, fingers on the page, one shaking her head, the other laughing. Twenty pairs like that, all at once. It's loud enough to sound like a train station. If you walked in without knowing, you'd think something had gone wrong. In a traditional Jewish house of study, this is the sound of something going right. Today on our visit to Judaism: why study itself can be holy, and why the arguing is part of it.
screen: `A ROOM OF LONG TABLES.` → `PAIRS, ARGUING OUT LOUD.` → `THE SOUND OF SOMETHING GOING RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Torah. In the narrowest sense it means the five books of Moses, the scroll in the ark of a synagogue. The Hebrew root has to do with teaching, pointing the way, so the word also stretches to mean all Jewish teaching, the whole conversation that grew around the scroll. That conversation has a famous first line. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a short book of sayings in the Mishnah, opens by tracing a chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and on to the teachers of the great assembly. Learning, in other words, is something handed from person to person, like a lamp passed down a line. The Torah itself asks for this. In Deuteronomy, right after the Shema we heard two days ago, it says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Teaching the young is not a hobby here; it sits inside the central prayer. Then the surprise. Jewish tradition honors argument. The Talmud records the debates of two ancient schools, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, who disagreed again and again. A heavenly voice, the story goes, declared that both were the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel partly because his students were humble and taught Shammai's view before their own. That's why study often happens in pairs, called chavruta, from the word for friend. You don't learn alone. You push, your partner pushes back, and the text opens.
screen: `TORAH — TEACHING, POINTING THE WAY.` · `A CHAIN FROM SINAI, HAND TO HAND.` · `TEACH THEM DILIGENTLY.` · `BOTH ARE WORDS OF THE LIVING GOD.` · then, large: `LEARN TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's a small practice. Take one line, any line you've met on this path, or the one from today: teach them diligently. Say it once, slowly. Now imagine a partner sitting across from you. What question would they ask about it? Who is them? What does diligently look like on a Tuesday? Let the question sit. You don't need an answer yet. The bell holds the time.
Torah. From a root about teaching and pointing the way: the five books of Moses, and the whole living conversation around them. Today's word.
Your line: learn together. Today, share one line with someone, a friend, a child, a coworker, and ask what they hear in it. Disagree kindly if you like. Day two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Jews study Torah and Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating line by line, and a weekly portion of the Torah is read in synagogue through the year.
